scope: NASA-reported Artemis II communications architecture and public lunar-flyby loss-of-signal and acquisition-of-signal timing used as an external validation target for MissionLab geocentric occultation geometry.

near_earth_network.name: Near Space Network
near_earth_network.role: NASA reports that the Near Space Network supported Artemis II during multiple stages of near-Earth mission operations.

deep_space_network.name: Deep Space Network
deep_space_network.role: NASA reports that primary communications support transitioned to the Deep Space Network after translunar injection for deep-space operations.

optical_demonstration.name: Orion Artemis II Optical Communications System
optical_demonstration.role: Separate optical communications demonstration flown concurrently with the mission's primary radio-frequency communications architecture.

public_lunar_occultation_window.reported_cause: Orion passes behind the Moon and the lunar body blocks the Earth-based Deep Space Network radio path.
public_lunar_occultation_window.interpretation: The public NASA window is an operational communications reference and validation target. It is not treated as an exact Earth-center geometric lunar-limb crossing.

sources.source_title: Artemis II Flight Day 6: Crew Ready for Lunar Flyby
claims_used: Mission control expected temporary loss of communication at 6:44 p.m. EDT.
Mission control expected communication reacquisition at 7:25 p.m. EDT.
Earthset and Earthrise occurred around the same lunar-flyby interval.

sources.source_title: Artemis II Flight Day 6: Lunar Flyby Updates
claims_used: Orion entered a planned communications blackout while passing behind the Moon.
NASA described the blackout as lasting about 40 minutes.
The lunar surface blocked radio signals from the Deep Space Network.

sources.source_title: Networks Keeping NASA's Artemis II Mission Connected
claims_used: Artemis II relied on the Near Space Network and Deep Space Network.
Primary communications support transitioned to the Deep Space Network following translunar injection.

sources.source_title: NASA's Orion Artemis II Optical Communications System
claims_used: O2O was an optical communications demonstration flown in parallel with Artemis II's primary communications systems.
O2O availability is distinct from the radio-frequency occultation geometry modeled in Phase 2G.1.

phase2g1_geometric_model.contact_definition: The Moon is between the Earth center and Orion and the perpendicular distance from the Moon center to the Earth-Orion line segment equals the adopted mean lunar radius.
limitations: Earth-center occultation is not equivalent to visibility from an individual Deep Space Network ground antenna.
The spherical mean-radius Moon ignores lunar topography and local limb relief.
The calculation is geometric and does not model antenna patterns, link margin, received signal strength, network scheduling, atmospheric effects, or operational handovers.
No light-time or stellar-aberration correction is applied to the geometric occultation test.
Radio-frequency lunar occultation is not equivalent to O2O optical-link availability.

validation_thresholds.interpretation: These are validation thresholds for consistency with a minute-level NASA operational timeline, not claims that Earth-center geometry should reproduce DSN station contact times exactly.

guardrails: Geometric lunar occultation does not by itself establish actual Deep Space Network link availability.
Earth-center line-of-sight geometry does not represent the topocentric geometry of an individual Deep Space Network antenna.
The NASA public loss-of-signal and acquisition-of-signal times are minute-level operational references, not exact geometric limb-contact measurements.
Radio-frequency occultation geometry is not used as a prediction of O2O optical-link availability.
No received signal strength, antenna gain, link margin, network scheduling, or communications performance is inferred from geometric occultation alone.
